items.title: Ernest "Punch" Miller Interview, 1959-08-20
items.q: So I come on and join Jack Carey. And I played with Jack a long climb, man.

ctx.x: Yeah, Dave Bailey. Yeah, well that's Ernest Johnson's brother. See? They must be half brother. But anyhow, they were always there, we were out in front of town there on Chippy Ward in St. Thomas. That's where they lived then. And what made me go out there, it was a boy out in the army, what he did now, I forget his name, but his mother lived out there and he told me to come and I could stay with him. That's how we were good friends in the army see? So he brought me there and they really treated me nice. I lived…
Well nobody's found it yet. I've heard talk of his record. He's supposed to have made, but you never know.

items.title: Ernest "Punch" Miller Interview, 1957-multiple
items.q: Some people hired Jack Carey to go to Birmingham and play for a night. Yeah, one night and a day. That's how it was, one night and a day. And he'd give each man a hundred dollars a piece in transportation. So, Road Runners are so funny. When Jack Carey got ready to pay us off

ctx.x: More funny than singing, I guess.

He tickled me one time. Some people hired Jack Carey to go to Birmingham and play for a night. Yeah, one night and a day. That's how it was, one night and a day. And he'd give each man a hundred dollars a piece in transportation. So, Road Runners are so funny. When Jack Carey got ready to pay us off, he asked Jack, say, you gonna give that clan that play a hundred dollars? So, Jack said, yeah, why? He said, man, give me half of his money because I'm sitting up there playing all that nice banjo and he's sitting up…
How many years were you with Carey?

items.title: Ernest "Punch" Miller Interview, 1959-09-01
items.q: Well, Jack Kerry was doing it. See, he had the band. He was paying us nice, see.

ctx.x: And you also played at what, the National Park or Third and Wall? National Park, yeah.

You know all. That was Third and Willow. It's a school there now, big school. But it used to be a great big baseball park, see. And we didn't have nothing but a little shit over us. What did you play? Concerts or for dances? Dancers. For dances, huh? Yeah. She'd be loaded at them. Well, who would pay you for that? Well, Jack Kerry was doing it. See, he had the band. He was paying us nice, see. Shills, I, I, he wouldn't lie because he was so kind of dumb himself. And he couldn't do nothing but come clean, see. And…
Well, how far away could they hear you when you were at 3rd and Willow?

items.title: Ernest "Punch" Miller Interview, 1971-04-08
items.q: I was playing, I joined his bands, and he gave me a place to stay there.

ctx.x: Where were you staying then? In a boarding house?

No, I was living in a place called Jack Kerry. He had a wooden coal place, and I was playing, I joined his bands, and he gave me a place to stay there. But it was pretty sad, though. Yeah. Oh, no, it was sad. It was sad.
How much did Jack call you, charge you to stay there?
